sections.body:
This is a story about Wren. Wren is a very small brown bird. She has a round head and a short tail.

Every good story has three parts. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning tells you who the story is about. The middle is where something goes wrong. The end is where everything comes right again.

Wren's story begins in a warm nest. The nest sits in an apple tree, right above the garden wall.

The middle is the part where Wren is too afraid. Her wings are small. Her friends are already flying high. She tries, and she falls, and she wants to give up.

The end is the surprise. Wren does not learn to fly the way she planned at all. She learns it by accident, on a frightening afternoon, and it turns out to be the best day of her life.

This story is about small steps. Watch how many small ones Wren takes before the sky opens up.
examples: This is the beginning of Wren's story.
The middle is the part where Wren feels afraid.
The end is the part where Wren flies.
sections.heading: A small bird with big plans

sections.body:
Every morning the birds sang in the apple tree. Wren sang too, but only from inside the nest.

On one warm morning, the birds all flew away at once. They went up over the roof, up over the church, up where the morning is still blue.

Wren watched them. She flapped her small wings hard, just to see how it felt.

"I want to do that," she said.

Her friend Sky landed on the branch beside her. Sky was older. Sky's wings were long and shiny.

"Everybody wants to," said Sky. "But look where they went. They left the branch one small step at a time. First they sat on the low branch. Then they sat on the roof. Then they flew."

"I am afraid of falling," said Wren.

"Everybody is," said Sky. "But you can only be afraid and flap at the same time. You cannot wait for the fear to go."

So Wren practised. She flapped on the branch until her wings ached. She jumped to the low branch, and back again. She jumped to the low branch, and stayed there longer each time.

On the third day, Wren was ready to try the roof. The roof was far. Very far.

"I will do it tomorrow," said Wren, and she went back to the nest to sleep.
examples: First they sat on the low branch. Then they sat on the roof.
You cannot wait for the fear to go.
sections.heading: The morning Wren watched the others fly

sections.body:
The next afternoon, the wind woke up.

The apple tree shook. The nest tipped. Wren rolled out of it, and the nest fell with a soft thump into the grass.

Wren fell too. Down and down, past the wall, past the shed, past the washing line. The garden came up to meet her very fast.

And then something wonderful happened. The air pushed under her wings. Her wings went out wide, on their own, and held the air like a boat holds water.

She did not fall. She slid. She slid over the grass, over the wall and up, up, up.

The wind carried her. She was not flying yet, not really. She was gliding, and gliding is when you do not flap but you still travel through the air.

"Sky!" she called. "Sky, look at me!"

Sky was laughing in the tree, but her eyes were bright too.

"Now," said Sky, "flap."

Wren flapped. One hard flap, and then another. And with every flap she went higher, and higher, and higher.

She flew over the roof. She flew over the church. She went up where the morning is still blue.

And the cat on the wall below looked up and said nothing at all, because a bird in the air is a bird nobody argues with.
examples: She slid over the grass, over the wall and up.
A bird in the air is a bird nobody argues with.
sections.heading: The fall that changed everything

sections.body:
Wren did not learn in one jump. She learned in small steps, and every small step made the next one easier.

You can use these steps for anything that feels too big to begin.
examples: I will try one small step today.
I am afraid, and I am doing it anyway.
Show me how you do it, please.
sections.heading: How Wren learned to fly
steps: Start where your feet are. Stay on the safe place and practise.
Move one small step further than yesterday, and no more.
Stay there until it feels ordinary, not exciting.
Be afraid and do it anyway. Fear does not have to leave first.
Ask someone who has done it to show you how.
Let the day surprise you. Sometimes the best step is not the one you planned.

sections.body:
These are the new words in this story. Read them once, then read the story again and find them.

A **nest** is the little home a bird builds out of twigs and grass. It is warm, and it holds the eggs.

A **branch** is the long arm of a tree. Birds sit on branches and sing from them.

To **flutter** is to move your wings quickly but not very far. A fluttering bird stays in one place.

To **glide** is to travel through the air without flapping. The wind holds you up while you glide.
sections.heading: The words in Wren's story

terms.gloss: The long arm of a tree. Birds sit on branches and sing from them.

terms.gloss: To move your wings quickly but not very far. A fluttering bird stays in the same place.

sections.body:
That evening, Wren did not sleep in the nest. The nest was in the grass now. She sat on the branch instead, and she practised flapping until the sun went down.

The lesson in this story is small, and it is worth keeping. The sky does not open all at once. It opens one step at a time, and the step you think is too small still counts.

But there is a second half to the lesson. Wren's best flight was not the one she practised for. It was the one the wind gave her when she was not ready. So practice your steps. And when the day shakes your nest, hold your wings open.
examples: The sky opens one step at a time.
The step you think is too small still counts.
sections.heading: What Wren learned

item.summary: Wren watches the other birds fly and wants to fly too, but she is afraid of falling. Follow her from the branch to the sky. You will learn the three parts of the story, four new words, and the small step that helped her leave the nest.
item.title: The Little Bird Who Wanted to Fly
